key_terms.meaning: Half-wave Vdc = Vm/π = 0.318 Vm; centre-tap and bridge Vdc = 2Vm/π = 0.637 Vm.
Bridge and half-wave diode: Vm; centre-tap diode: 2Vm; half-wave with capacitor: 2Vm.
FF = Vrms/Vdc; RF = √(FF² − 1): 1.21 half-wave, 0.482 full-wave, 0.042 three-phase bridge.
Vr = Idc/(2fC) full wave, Idc/(fC) half wave; Vdc ≈ Vm − Vr/2.
Lc = R/(3ω); an L-C filter needs L > Lc for continuous current; RF = √2/(12ω²LC).
Two diodes and two capacitors give 2Vm at no load; full-wave doubler ripple ≈ Idc/(fC) at 2f.
Vdc = (3√2/π) VL = 1.35 VL; ripple at 6f; PIV = √2 VL; distortion factor 3/π.
Delay from the natural firing point (where a diode would conduct) to the gate pulse.
Vdc = (2Vm/π) cos α with continuous current; (Vm/π)(1 + cos α) with R or with a half-controlled bridge.
Vdc = (3√2 VL/π) cos α = 1.35 VL cos α; α counted from 30° after the phase zero crossing.
Vdc = 1.17 Vph cos α; needs a neutral.
PF = g × cos φ1, with g = I1/Is: 0.900 cos α (1-phase bridge), 0.955 cos α (3-phase bridge).
1-phase: cos α − cos(α + μ) = 2ωLs Id/Vm; 3-phase: = 2ωLs Id/(√2 VL).
ΔVd = 2ωLs Id/π (1-phase bridge), 3ωLs Id/π (3-phase bridge); Vdc = Vd0 cos α − ΔVd.
γ = 180° − (α + μ) ≥ γ0 > ωtq; α_max from cos α_max = 2ωLs Id/(√2 VL) − cos γ0.
Two bridges in inverse parallel with α1 + α2 = 180°; four-quadrant operation.
Re = Vs²/P: what a PFC rectifier looks like to the mains; boost duty D = 1 − |vs|/Vo.

takeaways: A diode rectifier's average output is fixed by the supply peak and the circuit: Vm/π, 2Vm/π or 1.35 VL.
A capacitor filter lifts the output towards Vm with ripple Idc/(2fC), at the cost of narrow, peaky diode currents.
Doublers give 2Vm without a transformer; the three-phase bridge gives a stiff DC with 4 % ripple at 6f.
Phase control sets Vdc = Vd0 cos α for continuous current; discontinuous current always gives more than this.
In three-phase circuits α is counted from the crossing of two phase voltages, 30° after the phase zero crossing.
Power factor is distortion factor times displacement factor; cos α alone is never the whole answer.
Source inductance makes the devices overlap: the output drops by 2ωLs Id/π or 3ωLs Id/π, and μ grows with current.
Inversion needs α above 90°, a DC source and continuous current; α + μ must stay below 180° − γ0.
A dual converter gives all four quadrants, with a dead time or an intergroup reactor to stop a short circuit between the bridges.
A PFC rectifier makes the input current follow the voltage, so the mains sees a resistor and the power factor is near 1.
bank_note: Most syllabi ask for the derivation of the average output of a named converter with sketched waveforms, followed by a numerical on power factor, overlap or the inverter angle limit. Many papers set one question on the dual converter's modes and one comparing half-controlled and fully controlled bridges.

bank.q: Explain the single-phase diode bridge rectifier with a resistive load. Derive Vdc, Vrms, form factor, ripple factor, rectification efficiency and TUF, and state the PIV. Evaluate them for 230 V, 50 Hz and R = 100 Ω.
outline: Circuit and the conducting pairs in each half-cycle
answer: Circuit. Four diodes: D1 (from AC node A to DC+), D3 (B to DC+), D4 (DC− to A) and D2 (DC− to B), with R between DC+ and DC−. When A is positive, D1 and D2 conduct and the current flows down through R; when B is positive, D3 and D4 conduct and the current again flows down through R. The output is |vs|, two pulses per cycle.

answer.text: Average and RMS. With vs = Vm sin θ the output repeats every π:
answer.pre:
Vdc = (1/π) ∫₀^π Vm sin θ dθ = (Vm/π)[−cos θ]₀^π = 2Vm/π = 0.637 Vm
Vrms² = (1/π) ∫₀^π Vm² sin²θ dθ = (Vm²/π)(π/2) = Vm²/2  →  Vrms = Vm/√2

answer.text: Ratios.

answer: PIV. When D1 and D2 conduct, D3 is connected across the supply through D1 and D4 through D2, so each off diode blocks the full Vm: PIV = Vm.
TUF. The secondary carries a sine current of RMS Is = Vm/(√2 R), so its VA rating is Vs Is = Vm²/(2R) while Pdc = (2Vm/π)²/R. TUF = (4/π²) × 2 = 0.811.

answer.text: Numbers for 230 V, 50 Hz, R = 100 Ω.

answer: Comparison. A centre-tap rectifier gives the same Vdc with two diodes, but each blocks 2Vm and the transformer needs a centre tap; its TUF is about 0.69 against 0.81. The bridge is therefore preferred except at low voltage and high current, where one diode drop instead of two matters.

answer.text: Against the half-wave rectifier on the same supply.

answer: Sketch. Draw vs as a sine of peak 325 V. Below it draw vo = |vs|, which touches zero every 10 ms, with the average 207 V as a dashed line. Mark D1, D2 under the first hump and D3, D4 under the second. The voltage across D1 is zero while it conducts and follows vs during the second hump, reaching −325 V: that is the PIV.
Check. Pdc/Pac = (2.07² × 100)/(2.30² × 100) = 4.288/5.29 = 0.811, the same efficiency found from the formula.

bank.q: Explain the capacitor-input and choke-input (L-C) filters for a full-wave rectifier. Derive the ripple of the capacitor filter, define critical inductance, and compare the two for a 230 V bridge supplying 2 A.
outline: Capacitor charges to Vm and feeds the load in the gaps
Critical inductance Lc = R/(3ω) and the bleeder
answer: Capacitor filter. C across the load charges to Vm near each peak. When the rectified voltage falls below vC all diodes turn off and C alone supplies the load, its voltage falling almost linearly; it is recharged at the next peak.

answer.text: Ripple. If RC is much longer than the ripple period, C supplies Idc for nearly the whole gap of 1/(2f):
answer.pre:
charge lost per gap ΔQ = Idc × 1/(2f)
Vr = ΔQ/C = Idc/(2fC)          (peak to peak)
Vdc ≈ Vm − Vr/2;   Vac(rms) = Vr/(2√3);   RF = 1/(4√3 f C R)

answer: Diode current. The charge Idc/(2f) enters in the short interval before each peak, so the diode current is a tall pulse many times Idc. In the bridge each diode still blocks Vm; in a half-wave circuit with a capacitor the off diode sees vC + Vm, so its PIV is 2Vm.

answer.text: Choke-input filter. L in series and C across the load. The output stays near the average of the rectified wave, Vdc = 2Vm/π, and the ripple is the 2f term reduced by the L-C divider:
answer.pre:
RF = √2/(12 ω² L C)     (full wave, continuous choke current)
Lc = R/(3ω)              (critical inductance)

answer: Critical inductance. The choke current must not fall to zero, or the filter behaves like a capacitor filter and the output rises towards Vm. L must exceed Lc = R/(3ω); a bleeder resistor sets a minimum current so this holds at no load.

answer.text: Numbers: 230 V bridge, 2 A, C = 1000 µF; and R = 100 Ω, L = 0.2 H, C = 1000 µF.

answer: Sizing the capacitor. To hold the ripple of the 2 A load below 10 V p-p, C ≥ Idc/(2f Vr) = 2/(2 × 50 × 10) = 2000 µF. Doubling C halves the ripple but makes the charging pulses even narrower and taller.

Comparison. The capacitor filter gives the higher voltage (near Vm) and suits light loads, but its ripple grows with current and its peaky diode current gives a poor input power factor. The L-C filter gives a lower voltage (2Vm/π) that barely changes with load once L > Lc, smooth current in the diodes and much smaller ripple, at the cost of a heavy 50 Hz choke.
Check. A step-by-step simulation of the capacitor case gives 17.9 V of ripple, a little below the 20 V estimate, because C is recharged about 19° before each peak; the formula errs on the safe side.

bank.q: Define form factor, ripple factor, displacement factor, distortion factor, harmonic factor and power factor of a rectifier. Show that PF = g cos φ1 and evaluate all of them for a single-phase fully controlled bridge on 230 V carrying a level 10 A at α = 30°.
answer: Output side. Form factor FF = Vrms/Vdc. Ripple factor RF = Vac/Vdc = √(FF² − 1), where Vac is the RMS of the AC part of the output.

Input side. With Is the RMS input current and I1 the RMS of its fundamental, lagging the voltage by φ1: displacement factor DF = cos φ1; distortion factor g = I1/Is; harmonic factor HF = √(Is² − I1²)/I1 (the THD).

answer.text: Power factor. With a sinusoidal voltage only the fundamental current carries average power:
answer.pre:
P = Vs I1 cos φ1;   S = Vs Is
PF = P/S = (I1/Is) cos φ1 = g × DF
and HF = √(1/g² − 1)

answer.text: Full bridge, continuous current. The input current is a square wave of height Id lagging by α. Its Fourier fundamental:
Numbers (Id = 10 A, α = 30°, Vs = 230 V).

answer: Output side numbers. With continuous current Vdc = 207.07 × 0.866 = 179.33 V and Vrms = Vm/√2 = 230 V, so FF = 230/179.33 = 1.283 and RF = √(1.283² − 1) = 0.803. The ripple factor rises with α because Vdc falls while Vrms stays 230 V.

answer.text: Harmonic currents. For the square wave In = I1/n with odd n only:
answer.pre:
I3 = 9.003/3 = 3.00 A   I5 = 1.80 A   I7 = 1.29 A   I9 = 1.00 A
RMS of all harmonics = √(Is² − I1²) = √(100 − 81.05) = 4.35 A
HF = 4.35/9.003 = 0.483, the value found from g

answer.text: Typical output-side values (resistive load, α = 0).

answer: Why two factors. The distortion factor g depends only on the shape of the current, so it stays 0.900 for any α while the current is a square wave. The displacement factor depends only on the delay. Turning the output down therefore lowers the power factor through cos α alone: at α = 60° the same bridge has PF = 0.900 × 0.5 = 0.450.
Check. DC power Vdc Id = 179.33 × 10 = 1793 W equals the AC power found from the fundamental, and P/S = 1793/2300 = 0.780 agrees with g × DF.

bank.q: Explain the single-phase dual converter. Derive the firing-angle condition, describe the circulating-current and non-circulating modes, and show the four quadrants of operation.
outline: Two fully controlled bridges in inverse parallel
V1 = (2Vm/π) cos α1, V2 = −(2Vm/π) cos α2
Non-circulating: one bridge gated, dead time
answer: Circuit. Converter P and converter N, each a single-phase fully controlled bridge, are connected to the same DC load in inverse parallel: P can push current +Id into the load, N can push −Id. Each needs continuous current for its cosine law.

answer.text: Firing condition. Measured with the same load polarity:
answer.pre:
V1 = (2Vm/π) cos α1          (converter P)
V2 = −(2Vm/π) cos α2         (converter N, connected the other way)
V1 = V2  →  cos α1 = −cos α2  →  α1 + α2 = 180°

answer: Example. On 230 V with α1 = 30°: V1 = 207.07 × 0.866 = 179.33 V, so α2 = 150° and N's own output is 207.07 × cos 150° = −179.33 V, which is +179.33 V at the load.

Non-circulating mode. Only one bridge receives gate pulses. To reverse, the controller removes P's pulses, waits until the load current is zero and P's thyristors have recovered (a dead time of a few milliseconds), then fires N. No reactor is needed; torque is lost during the dead time.

Circulating-current mode. Both bridges are gated with α1 + α2 = 180°. Their averages are equal but their instantaneous voltages differ (different ripple shapes), and this difference drives a current round the P–N loop. An intergroup reactor, split as Lr/2 in each path, limits it. Current can then reverse smoothly with no dead time; the cost is the reactor, extra losses and larger thyristor ratings.

answer.text: Four quadrants.
Pairs of firing angles on 230 V.

answer: Uses. Reversible DC drives that must brake and reverse quickly: rolling mills, hoists, lifts, excavators and machine-tool spindles. A single-phase unit suits small drives; large ones use two three-phase bridges with the same logic.

Why both bridges cannot simply be gated together. With no reactor, the ripple difference would drive a current limited only by the supply inductance through two thyristors of each bridge: a short circuit. One of the two modes is always used.
Check. At α1 = 90° both bridges give zero average, and α2 = 90° too: the zero-speed point where the drive passes from quadrant I to quadrant II or IV.

bank.q: A single-phase fully controlled bridge feeds a highly inductive load. Derive Vdc = (2Vm/π) cos α and the RMS output, sketch the output for α = 30°, 90° and 150°, and find Vdc and Id on 230 V for α = 30° with an RLE load of R = 2 Ω and E = 100 V.
outline: Conduction of T1, T2 from α to π + α
Positive, zero and negative averages; 150° needs a DC source
answer: Conduction. T1 and T2 are fired at α and, because the inductance keeps the current flowing, stay on until T3 and T4 are fired at π + α. So for α < θ < π + α the output is vs = Vm sin θ, including the negative part between π and π + α.

answer.text: Average.
answer.pre:
Vdc = (1/π) ∫ from α to π+α of Vm sin θ dθ
    = (Vm/π)[−cos θ] from α to π+α
    = (Vm/π)[cos α − cos(π + α)] = (2Vm/π) cos α

answer.text: RMS.
answer.pre: Vrms² = (1/π) ∫ from α to π+α of Vm² sin²θ dθ = Vm²/2   →   Vrms = Vm/√2

answer.text: Waveforms on 230 V (2Vm/π = 207.07 V).

head: α
Output between firings
Vdc
Mode
rows: vs from 30° to 210°: a small negative slice after 180°
vs from 90° to 270°: equal positive and negative areas
inverter (needs a DC source in the load)

answer: Sketch. For each α draw the supply sine, mark the firing at α and π + α, and draw the output as the sine from α to π + α, then its mirror image from π + α to 2π + α. At 150° the load must contain a source of reversed polarity, because an RL load alone cannot keep the current flowing against a negative average.

answer.text: RLE load at α = 30°, R = 2 Ω, E = 100 V.
Ratings and supply side for this load.

answer: Check. The inductor drops no average voltage, so Vdc = E + Id R holds: 100 + 39.67 × 2 = 179.34 V. Vrms is 230 V at every α, so the form factor grows as α rises.

bank.q: Derive the average output of a three-phase fully controlled bridge with continuous current. For a 415 V, 50 Hz bridge at α = 45° carrying 50 A, find Vdc, the DC power, the thyristor ratings, the line current and the input power factor.
outline: Conducting pairs every 60°; output is a line voltage
α counted from 30° after the phase zero crossing
answer: Operation. One thyristor of the upper group (T1, T3, T5) and one of the lower group (T4, T6, T2) conduct at any time; a new one is fired every 60° in the order T1 to T6, so the load sees one line voltage for 60° at a time. With va = Vm sin θ, phase a becomes most positive at θ = 30°, so T1 is fired at 30° + α.

answer.text: Average. Pair T6T1 puts vab = √3 Vm sin(θ + 30°) on the load from 30° + α to 90° + α:
answer.pre:
Vdc = (3/π) ∫ from 30°+α to 90°+α of √3 Vm sin(θ + 30°) dθ
    = (3√3 Vm/π)[cos(60° + α) − cos(120° + α)]
    = (3√3 Vm/π) × 2 sin(90° + α) sin 30°   (difference of two cosines)
    = (3√3 Vm/π) cos α
With √3 Vm = √2 VL:  Vdc = (3√2 VL/π) cos α = 1.35 VL cos α

answer: Waveform. Draw the six line voltages vab, vac, vbc, vba, vca, vcb, each peaking 60° after the one before. With α = 45°, each pair takes over 45° after the crossing of two line voltages, so the output is a 60° slice of a line voltage running from 15° to 75° after its peak, on the falling side. At α = 45° it never dips below zero; the output first goes negative once α exceeds 60°.

answer.text: Numbers (415 V, α = 45°, Id = 50 A).

answer: Power factor by formula. The line current is 120° blocks shifted by α, so g = 3/π = 0.955 and DF = cos 45° = 0.707: PF = 0.955 × 0.707 = 0.675, the same as P/S.

Ripple and harmonics. Six pulses per cycle put the lowest output ripple at 300 Hz. With continuous current the output RMS is VLm √(1/2 + 3√3 cos 2α/(4π)), which is VLm/√2 = 415.0 V at α = 45°, so FF = 415.0/396.30 = 1.047 and RF = 0.311. On the AC side I1 = (√6/π) × 50 = 38.98 A, the 5th and 7th harmonics are 7.80 A and 5.57 A, and the reactive power is Q1 = √3 × 415 × 38.98 × sin 45° = 19.81 kvar, equal to P at this angle.
Check. At α = 0 the bridge becomes the diode bridge: 560.45 V, the value used for the three-phase diode rectifier on 415 V.

bank.q: Explain the effect of source inductance on a single-phase fully controlled bridge with level load current. Derive the overlap equation and the commutation drop, and find μ and Vdc on 230 V, 50 Hz with Ls = 5 mH, Id = 20 A and α = 30°.
outline: Ls prevents an instant current transfer
All four thyristors conduct during μ; vo = 0
answer: What happens. Before α, T3 and T4 carry Id and the supply current is −Id. When T1 and T2 are fired at α the supply current must reverse to +Id, but Ls allows only a finite di/dt. All four thyristors conduct together for the overlap angle μ, the bridge output is short-circuited (vo = 0) and the supply voltage appears across Ls.

answer.text: Overlap equation. During overlap vs = Ls dis/dt, with is going from −Id to +Id:
answer.pre:
∫ from α to α+μ of Vm sin θ dθ = ωLs ∫ dis = ωLs × 2Id
Vm [cos α − cos(α + μ)] = 2ωLs Id

answer.text: Commutation drop. Without Ls the output would follow vs during μ; that area is lost once per half-cycle (π):
answer.pre:
lost area = ∫ from α to α+μ of Vm sin θ dθ = 2ωLs Id
ΔVd = 2ωLs Id/π
Vdc = (2Vm/π) cos α − 2ωLs Id/π = (Vm/π)[cos α + cos(α + μ)]

answer.text: Numbers.

answer: Effects. The output falls linearly with load current (an equivalent resistance Rc = 2ωLs/π = 1.0 Ω that wastes no power), the supply voltage is notched twice per cycle, and in inverter mode the overlap reduces the largest usable firing angle.

answer.text: Overlap at other angles (same Ls and Id, so 2ωLs Id/Vm = 0.1932).

answer: The same volt-second area 2ωLs Id is needed at every α, and near the voltage peak the supply delivers it fastest, so the overlap is longest at α = 0 and shortest near α = 90°. The commutation drop of 20.0 V does not change with α; at 20 A it takes 11 % off the 179.33 V that the bridge would give without Ls.

Sketch. The output follows vs from α + μ to π + α and sits at zero during each overlap; the supply current ramps from −20 A to +20 A over μ instead of jumping, so its edges are sloped and the current wave is a trapezoid.

bank.q: Explain the full-wave and half-wave voltage doublers and the three-phase diode bridge. Find the output of a full-wave doubler on 12 V rms with two 1000 µF capacitors supplying 50 mA, and the voltages and currents of a 415 V three-phase bridge feeding 20 Ω through a large inductor.
outline: Full-wave doubler: C1 and C2 each charged to Vm, in series
Half-wave doubler: clamp plus peak detector, ripple at f
answer: Full-wave doubler. Two equal capacitors in series across the load, their midpoint joined to one supply terminal. D1 charges C1 to Vm on the positive half-cycle and D2 charges C2 to Vm on the negative one. The load sees 2Vm at no load. Each capacitor carries the load current for a whole cycle before it is recharged, so the output ripple is Idc/(fC) at 2f and the average is about 2Vm − Idc/(fC).

Half-wave doubler. C1 in series with the supply and D1 across the line form a clamp: C1 charges to Vm on the negative half-cycle. On the positive half the supply and C1 add, and D2 charges C2 to 2Vm. One terminal is common to input and output, but C2 is recharged only once per cycle, so the ripple is at f.

answer.text: Doubler numbers (12 V, 1000 µF each, 50 mA).

answer: Three-phase bridge. Six diodes; the upper diode of the most positive phase and the lower diode of the most negative phase conduct, so the output is the top envelope of the six line voltages, a new pair every 60°, each diode on for 120°.

answer.text: Bridge numbers (415 V, R = 20 Ω, level current).

answer: Ripple of the three-phase bridge. The output swings between VLm cos 30° and VLm, so the ripple is 78.6 V p-p at 300 Hz on a 560 V average, and its RMS is 4.2 % of the average. A small inductor is enough to keep the current level.

Comparison. The doubler raises voltage without a transformer but only for small currents, since its output falls by 1/(fC) volts per ampere; the three-phase bridge gives high power with only 4.2 % ripple at 300 Hz and a power factor of 0.955.
Check. A step-by-step simulation of the doubler gives 33.0 V average and 0.9 V ripple, close to the estimates; for the bridge, P = 560.45 × 28.02 = 15.71 kW and 3/π = 0.955 agree.

bank.q: State the conditions for a phase-controlled converter to work as a line-commutated inverter. Explain the extinction angle and the inverter angle limit, and find α_max, μ and Vdc for a 400 V, 50 Hz three-phase bridge with Ls = 1 mH per phase, Id = 100 A and γ0 = 15°.
outline: Fully controlled converter, DC source, α > 90°, continuous current
Commutation failure if γ is too short
cos α_max = 2ωLs Id/(√2 VL) − cos γ0
answer: Conditions. (1) A fully controlled converter: diodes in a half-controlled bridge would clamp the output at zero. (2) A DC source (a machine running as a generator, a battery, an HVDC line) whose polarity drives current into the converter's positive terminal. (3) 90° < α < α_max with continuous current, so that Vdc = Vd0 cos α is negative while Id stays positive: power flows from DC to AC.

Extinction angle. After the overlap ends at α + μ the outgoing thyristor is reverse biased only until 180°, where the two commutating voltages cross. That interval γ = 180° − (α + μ) must exceed γ0, which is ωtq plus a safety margin (tq = 100 µs is 1.8° at 50 Hz).

Commutation failure. If γ < ωtq the outgoing thyristor has not recovered when its anode turns positive; it conducts again, the DC source is shorted through two thyristors of one leg, and the current rises until protection acts.

answer.text: Limit with overlap. Put α + μ = 180° − γ0 into the overlap equation:
answer.pre:
cos α − cos(α + μ) = 2ωLs Id/(√2 VL)
cos α_max + cos γ0 = 2ωLs Id/(√2 VL)
cos α_max = 2ωLs Id/(√2 VL) − cos γ0

answer.text: Numbers.

answer: Effect of current. At 20 A the same working gives cos α_max = 0.0222 − 0.9659 = −0.9437, α_max = 160.7°: the limit moves 12° closer to 90° as the current rises to 100 A, so practical inverters control γ, not a fixed α.

What the DC source must supply. If the DC circuit has R = 0.1 Ω, then for Id = 100 A at α_max the source must be E = Vdc − Id R = −491.8 − 10.0 = −501.8 V, that is 501.8 V with the reversed polarity. A source weaker than 491.8 V could not push 100 A into the inverter at this angle; the controller would have to move α back towards 90°.
Uses. Regenerative braking of DC drives, the inverter station of an HVDC link, and the return of energy from a hoist or a test rig to the mains.
Check. Vdc = (Vd0/2)(cos α − cos γ0) = 270.09 × (−0.8549 − 0.9659) = −491.8 V, the same as Vd0 cos α − ΔVd.

bank.q: Compare the single-phase half-controlled and fully controlled bridges for a DC motor drive on 230 V at α = 60° with a level 10 A: output voltage, input power factor, reactive power, ability to brake, and cost.
outline: Full: Vdc = (2Vm/π) cos α; half: (Vm/π)(1 + cos α)
Input current shapes: square wave vs 120° blocks
g and DF for each; PF numbers
Inversion and regenerative braking only in the full bridge

answer.text: Output voltage (continuous current).
answer.pre:
Full bridge:  Vdc = 207.07 × cos 60° = 103.54 V
Half-controlled:  Vdc = 103.54 × (1 + cos 60°) = 155.31 V

answer: The half-controlled bridge clamps the output at zero through its freewheeling path, so it never adds the negative slice and gives more voltage at the same α.

Input current. The full bridge draws a square wave of ±10 A lagging by α. The half-controlled bridge draws current only from α to π in each half-cycle: each block is 180° − α = 120° wide and is centred at (α + π)/2 = 120°, which is 30° after the voltage peak at 90°, so its fundamental lags the voltage by α/2 = 30°.

answer.text: Power factor.
Derivation of the half-controlled output. The output follows vs from α to π and is clamped at zero from π to π + α:
answer.pre: Vdc = (1/π) ∫ from α to π of Vm sin θ dθ = (Vm/π)(1 + cos α)

answer.text: Across the range of α (Id = 10 A). For the half-controlled bridge I1 = 0.9003 Id cos(α/2) and Is = Id √(1 − α/π):

answer: The gap widens as α rises: at α = 90° the full bridge draws only reactive power, while the half-controlled bridge still delivers 1035 W at PF = 0.637.
Power check. Full: Vdc Id = 103.54 × 10 = 1035 W. Half-controlled: 155.31 × 10 = 1553 W. Both equal the AC power found from the fundamental.

Braking. The full bridge can run at α > 90° and return energy when the motor's EMF is reversed (regenerative braking, quadrant IV). The half-controlled bridge cannot: its output is never negative, so braking needs a resistor or a contactor.
Cost. The half-controlled bridge uses two thyristors and two diodes and needs only two isolated gate drives; the full bridge needs four thyristors and four gate drives.

Verdict. For a one-direction drive that never brakes regeneratively (a fan, a pump, a conveyor) the half-controlled bridge is better: cheaper and with almost twice the power factor at mid-range speeds (0.827 against 0.450 here). For a hoist, a traction drive or anything that must return energy, only the fully controlled bridge will do.

bank.q: Analyse the input current harmonics of single-phase and three-phase fully controlled bridges with level DC current. Explain why the three-phase bridge has a better power factor at the same α, which harmonics appear, and how the power factor of phase-controlled converters can be improved.
outline: Square wave: I1 = 0.900 Id, odd harmonics, THD 48.3 %

answer.text: Single-phase bridge. The supply current is a square wave of height Id:
answer.pre:
In(peak) = 4Id/(nπ) for odd n;   I1 = 0.9003 Id;   Is = Id
g = 0.900;   THD = √(1/g² − 1) = 48.3 %
harmonics: 3, 5, 7, 9 … with In = I1/n

answer.text: Three-phase bridge. Each line carries +Id for 120°, zero for 60°, −Id for 120°, zero for 60°:
answer.pre:
Is = √(2/3) Id = 0.816 Id;   I1 = (√6/π) Id = 0.780 Id
g = 3/π = 0.955;   THD = 31.1 %
harmonics: 5, 7, 11, 13 … (no even, no triplen) with In = I1/n

answer: Why h = kp ± 1. Half-wave symmetry removes the even harmonics. In the three-phase bridge the 60° gaps also remove every multiple of 3, leaving 6k ± 1. In general a p-pulse converter has characteristic harmonics kp ± 1.

answer.text: Numbers at α = 30°.
Harmonic spectra (In = I1/n).

answer: Why the three-phase bridge is better. Its current is closer to a sine (g = 0.955 against 0.900), so for the same displacement factor cos α it has a higher power factor and lower THD; its lowest harmonic is the 5th, not the 3rd, which is easier to filter.

Improving the power factor. Both bridges have DF = cos α, so the power factor collapses at low output. Remedies: a freewheeling diode or a half-controlled bridge (DF = cos(α/2)); extinction angle control with self-commutated switches (leading current); symmetrical angle control (DF = 1); PWM control (harmonics pushed to high frequency); sequence control of two series bridges; shunt capacitors and tuned filters; or a PFC/active front end.

Raising the pulse number. Two six-pulse bridges fed from star and delta secondaries are shifted by 30°; their 5th and 7th harmonics cancel in the primary, so a twelve-pulse converter draws only h = 12k ± 1 (11, 13, 23, 25 …) and its output ripple is at 600 Hz. This is the usual arrangement for large drives and HVDC.
Check. In each case the AC power Vs I1 cos φ1 equals the DC power, so the numbers are consistent: 230 × 9.003 × 0.866 = 1793 W and √3 × 400 × 38.98 × 0.866 = 23.39 kW.

bank.q: Evaluate a diode bridge with a capacitor filter against a boost PFC rectifier as the front end of a 500 W, 230 V supply: input current, power factor, THD, DC bus regulation, size and cost.
outline: Capacitor-input: narrow pulses, PF 0.5 to 0.7, high THD
Boost PFC: iref = k|vs|, Re = Vs²/P
Numbers: 2.17 A, 3.07 A peak, D, ripple
Regulated 400 V bus vs unregulated peak
answer: Capacitor-input bridge. The capacitor holds the bus near the mains peak (about 325 V less half the ripple); the diodes conduct only for a few tens of degrees before each peak. The displacement factor is close to 1, but the current is a tall pulse, so the distortion factor is low, THD is often above 100 % and the power factor is typically 0.5 to 0.7. The bus voltage follows the mains and sags with load.

answer.text: Boost PFC. A boost cell after the bridge is switched so that the average inductor current follows iref = k|vs|. The mains then sees a resistor:
Bus. The slow voltage loop holds the bus at 400 V whatever the mains (within range) and load. The 100 Hz ripple on a 330 µF bus is
Comparison.
Inductor ripple across the half-cycle (L = 1 mH, 65 kHz, Vo = 400 V). ΔiL = |vs| D/(L fs) with D = 1 − |vs|/Vo:

answer: Hold-up. The regulated bus also stores energy for a mains dropout. Letting the 330 µF bus fall from 400 V to 300 V releases ½ × 330 × 10⁻⁶ × (400² − 300²) = 11.55 J, which carries 500 W for 23.1 ms, more than one full mains cycle.

Judgement. At 500 W the capacitor-input bridge would not meet the harmonic limits for computer-class equipment, draws an RMS current far above the 2.17 A needed, and makes the following converter work over a wide input range. The PFC stage costs more parts and a little efficiency, but gives a stable 400 V bus, smaller downstream components and a near-unity power factor. For anything above roughly 75 W connected to public mains the PFC rectifier is the right choice; below that, the plain bridge remains acceptable.
Check. Peak current from Re: 325.27/105.8 = 3.07 A, which agrees with √2 × 2.17; and Io = 500/400 = 1.25 A on the bus.

bank.q: Evaluate how source inductance affects a 400 V, 50 Hz three-phase bridge (Ls = 1 mH per phase) at light load (20 A) and heavy load (100 A), both as a rectifier at α = 0 and as an inverter with γ0 = 15°.
outline: μ at α = 0 from cos μ = 1 − 2ωLs Id/(√2 VL)

answer.text: Formulas.
answer.pre:
ΔVd = 3ωLs Id/π;   cos α − cos(α + μ) = 2ωLs Id/(√2 VL)
Vd0 = 3√2 × 400/π = 540.19 V;   ωLs = 0.3142 Ω
inverter limit: cos α_max = 2ωLs Id/(√2 VL) − cos γ0

answer.text: Rectifier at α = 0.

answer: Regulation. The output falls by 0.3 V per ampere (Rc = 3ωLs/π = 0.30 Ω), from 534.2 V to 510.2 V between the two loads: a 4.5 % drop with no power lost in Rc. A speed or voltage loop has to compensate by reducing α.

answer.text: Inverter with γ0 = 15°.

answer: Why the limit moves. The current transfer needs a fixed volt-second area 2ωLs Id; at 100 A that takes 16.3° near the end of the half-cycle, so α must be 12° earlier than at 20 A to leave the same 15° of reverse bias. A controller set to α = 155° would work at 20 A and fail at 100 A.

Rectifier at α = 30°, 100 A. cos(30° + μ) = 0.8660 − 0.1111 = 0.7549, so 30° + μ = 41.0° and μ = 11.0°, much shorter than the 27.3° at α = 0 because the commutating voltage is larger at the instant of firing. Vdc = 540.19 × 0.866 − 30.0 = 437.8 V.

Equivalent circuit. The bridge behaves as a source Vd0 cos α behind Rc = 0.30 Ω. The line current loses its sharp edges: each 120° block becomes a trapezoid with sloped sides μ wide, which lowers the higher harmonics a little.

Consequences for design. (1) Notches on the supply grow with μ, so heavy drives need line reactors or their own transformer. (2) The inverter must be controlled on γ (constant extinction angle control) or limited to α_max at the highest current. (3) Some Ls is wanted: it limits di/dt and fault current. So Ls is chosen, not simply minimised.
Check. Vdc at the 100 A limit by the second form: (Vd0/2)(cos α − cos γ0) = 270.09 × (−0.8549 − 0.9659) = −491.8 V.

bank.q: A 415 V, 50 Hz three-phase dual converter supplies a DC motor (Ra = 0.5 Ω). Find the firing angles for forward motoring at 50 A with E = 400 V and for regenerative braking at 50 A at the same speed, and explain how the controller changes over between the bridges.
outline: Motoring: Vt = E + Id Ra; α1 from cos α1 = Vt/Vd0
Braking: Id reverses through N; Vt = E − Id Ra
answer: Base value. Vd0 = 3√2 × 415/π = 560.45 V for each bridge.

answer.text: Forward motoring through P (quadrant I).
Regenerative braking through N (quadrant II). The speed and E are unchanged but the current reverses, so it must flow through N:
answer.pre:
Vt = E + Id Ra = 400 + (−50)(0.5) = 375 V   (motor terminals, same polarity)
N's own output = −375 V  →  cos αN = −375/560.45 = −0.6691  →  αN = 132.0°
Power returned = 375 × 50 = 18.75 kW

answer: Power balance in braking. The machine converts 400 × 50 = 20.0 kW of mechanical power, the armature loses 50² × 0.5 = 1.25 kW, and 18.75 kW returns to the supply through N.

answer.text: Changeover (non-circulating mode).

head: Step
Action
rows: Speed loop asks for negative torque; current reference reverses
Remove P's pulses (or drive α1 towards the inverter limit to force the current down)
Zero-current detector confirms Id = 0; wait a dead time for P's thyristors to recover
Release N at a safe large angle and reduce αN until it gives −375 V, here 132.0°
N regulates −50 A until the speed has fallen; at reversal N moves to α < 90° (quadrant III)

answer.text: Supply side in the two modes. Line current √(2/3) × 50 = 40.82 A, I1 = 38.98 A, S = √3 × 415 × 40.82 = 29.34 kVA in both:

answer: The converter draws reactive power in both modes, even while it returns real power: a phase-controlled bridge always takes lagging current.

Circulating-current alternative. Both bridges stay gated with αP + αN = 180° (here 40.7° and 139.3° before the change), and an intergroup reactor limits the loop current; the torque then reverses without a dead time, at the price of the reactor and extra losses.
Check. In braking N works inside its inverter range: with no overlap α_max is about 180° − γ0, far above 132°, so commutation is safe; and Vt = Vd0 |cos αN| = 560.45 × 0.6691 = 375 V.

glossary.def: Circuit that converts AC to DC.
Mean of the output voltage over one period.
RMS value divided by average value.
RMS of the AC ripple divided by the average output.
Largest reverse voltage across an off diode or thyristor.
DC output power divided by the transformer's VA rating.
Diode across an inductive load that carries its current when the supply reverses, clamping the output at zero.
Shunt capacitor that holds the output near the peak voltage.
Least choke inductance, R/(3ω) for full wave, that keeps an L-C filter's current continuous.
Two diodes and two capacitors that give about twice the supply peak.
Number of output pulses per supply cycle; the lowest ripple is at p f.
Delay from the natural firing point to the gate pulse.
Instant at which a diode in the same position would start conducting.
Angle β at which the load current of a half-wave RL circuit falls to zero.
Bridge of thyristors and diodes; output never negative.
Bridge of thyristors only; can invert with a DC source in the load.
Load current never falls to zero between firings.
Cosine of the angle between the fundamental input current and the voltage.
Fundamental RMS current divided by total RMS current.
RMS of all harmonics divided by the fundamental; the THD.
Angle during which the outgoing and incoming devices conduct together because of source inductance.
ΔVd/Id: models the overlap drop; dissipates no power.
Reverse-bias time of the outgoing thyristor in inversion, 180° − (α + μ).
Outgoing thyristor conducts again in inversion, shorting the DC source through one leg.
Two fully controlled bridges in inverse parallel for four-quadrant operation.
Inductor between the bridges of a dual converter that limits circulating current.
Vs²/P: the resistance a PFC rectifier presents to the mains.
Shaping the input current into a sine in phase with the voltage.
